openingProblem.problem: Soviet control of eastern Europe lasted more than forty years. In the second half of 1989 it collapsed in six countries in a few months, mostly without a shot being fired. Was it pushed from below, or released from above?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: did the people of eastern Europe overthrow Soviet control, or did Moscow let it go?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Moscow lets go: Gorbachev and the bankrupt satellites
chunks.body:
The collapse of 1989 began in Moscow. From 1985, Tony Judt writes, the Soviet Union "progressively removed itself from direct oversight of its client states". The regimes still had their police and informers, but they could no longer be sure that Soviet tanks would rescue them. On 7 December 1988 Mikhail Gorbachev told the United Nations that he was cutting Soviet forces in Europe and that "freedom of choice is a universal principle. There should be no exceptions." Judt calls this more than a renunciation of the Brezhnev Doctrine: it was "immediately understood" to mean that the peoples of the satellites could go their own way, socialist or not.

The second cause was bankruptcy. In the 1970s the regimes had borrowed in the West to keep their people supplied. **Poland** was the extreme case. Martial law had suppressed Solidarity but solved nothing; after it, Western condemnation meant Poland could no longer borrow its way out. Its debt was approaching $40 billion. The regime raised prices by 25 per cent in 1987 and 60 per cent in 1988, and, as in 1970, 1976 and 1980, strikes followed. Inflation was approaching 1,000 per cent a year.

Meanwhile society had survived martial law. Lech Wałęsa was released in November 1982 and won the Nobel Peace Prize the next year. When the political police murdered the radical priest Jerzy Popiełuszko in 1984, 350,000 people came to his funeral. By the mid-1980s, Judt says, Poland faced "a stand-off between a recalcitrant society and an increasingly desperate state".

In August 1988 the Interior Minister, General Kiszczak, did something unthinkable: he asked Wałęsa, leader of a banned union, to help end the strikes. This mattered because the regime was admitting that it could not govern without its opponents, which meant that negotiation, not repression, became the way out. A week after Gorbachev's UN speech, Solidarity formed a committee to prepare for full negotiations.

Judt is careful not to make Gorbachev the only cause. Economic failure and society's resistance had been building for years. But the satellites' rulers had always relied on the final guarantee of Soviet force. When Moscow withdrew it, the regimes had to face their people with nothing but their own failures.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev's renunciation of force removed the final guarantee of the satellite regimes.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The regimes still had their own police; Honecker and Ceauşescu were ready to use force.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Economic bankruptcy, especially debt, left the regimes unable to buy calm.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Romania paid off its debt and still fell, so debt alone was not the cause.

argumentsThatWork.claim: In Poland society outlasted martial law, forcing the regime to negotiate.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The opposition was cautious and self-limiting; it was the regime that chose to talk.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent was Gorbachev responsible for the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe in 1989?
Discuss the view that the collapse of Communism in eastern Europe in 1989 was caused by economic failure.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Gorbachev's renunciation of force was the decisive cause of the collapse of Soviet control, because it removed the regimes' final guarantee.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 7 December 1988 he told the United Nations that 'freedom of choice is a universal principle', which Judt says was immediately understood to let the satellites go their own way.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that rulers facing strikes and debt, as in Poland, could no longer count on Soviet tanks, so they had to negotiate with their opponents.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the economic crisis and the opposition had been building for years: Poland's debt was approaching $40 billion before 1989.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Gorbachev was therefore the decisive cause, but only because the regimes were already too weak to survive without Soviet force.

chunks.title: Negotiated exits: Poland and Hungary
chunks.body:
In Poland and Hungary the regimes negotiated their own departure. On 6 February 1989 the Polish Communists recognised Solidarity as a negotiating partner and opened **Round Table** talks. On 5 April they agreed to legalise independent unions and hold elections to a new Assembly. The elections of **4 June 1989** were designed to protect the party: the Senate was open, but a guaranteed share of the seats in the lower house, the Sejm, was reserved for the Communists. The result shocked everyone. Solidarity won 99 of the 100 Senate seats and every Sejm seat it was allowed to contest; only two Communist candidates on the reserved list won the 50 per cent they needed.

The regime could have ignored the vote or declared martial law again. Instead, Gorbachev told Jaruzelski privately that the election must stand. In late summer 1989 **Tadeusz Mazowiecki** became the first non-Communist prime minister in post-war Poland. Solidarity made Jaruzelski head of state to ease the transition. On 29 December the party's "leading role" was removed from the constitution, and on 27 January 1990 the party dissolved itself.

In **Hungary** the Communists dismantled their own system. In May 1988 younger reformers, inspired by Gorbachev, removed the 76-year-old Kádár. In November 1988 independent parties were permitted; in 1989 the legislature approved a transition to a multi-party system, and an official inquiry redefined 1956 as a "popular uprising". On **16 June 1989**, the anniversary of his execution, Imre Nagy was reburied as a national hero. About 300,000 people lined the streets; the young Viktor Orbán spoke at the graveside. Judt calls the reburial "an admission of defeat", an acknowledgement that the party had lived a lie. On 23 October the country was renamed simply the Hungarian Republic. It was, Judt notes, the only exit from Communism "effected entirely from within".

Hungary's reform also undid its neighbour. On 2 May 1989 Hungary removed the electrified fence on its border with Austria. East Germans began to arrive as "tourists": 25,000 by July, 60,000 by early September. On 10 September Foreign Minister Gyula Horn announced that they would be let through, and within 72 hours some 22,000 had crossed. When East Berlin protested, Budapest replied that it was bound by the Helsinki Final Act. This mattered because a hole had opened in the Iron Curtain, which meant that the East German regime could no longer keep its people in.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Poland and Hungary ended Communism by negotiation, not revolution.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Mass strikes in Poland forced the negotiations, so pressure from below mattered.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Gorbachev's refusal to back force made the Polish election result stand.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Jaruzelski also judged force would fail; the choice was Polish too.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Hungary's opening of its border broke the GDR.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The East German regime's own rigidity, rigging votes in May 1989, made its people want to leave.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the party's claim to represent the people was destroyed in a vote it had designed itself, so it could not credibly keep power.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the party could still have used force; it was Gorbachev's insistence that the election must stand that removed that option.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Poland's exit was therefore negotiated in form, but decided by Moscow's refusal to back repression.

chunks.title: Autumn 1989: Berlin, Prague, Bucharest and Sofia
chunks.body:
The hard-line regimes fell next. In **East Germany** Erich Honecker refused to reform. His regime rigged local elections in May 1989 to show 98.85 per cent support. As East Germans fled through Hungary, dissidents founded New Forum, and Monday demonstrations in Leipzig grew from 10,000 on 2 October to 90,000 and then 300,000. On 7 October, at the GDR's fortieth anniversary, Gorbachev warned Honecker that "life punishes those who delay". On 18 October Egon Krenz and other colleagues removed Honecker. On 4 November half a million people gathered in Berlin. On the evening of **9 November** Politburo member Günter Schabowski announced on live television that travel to the West was allowed with immediate effect. Within hours 50,000 people had crossed into West Berlin. The rulers had hoped to release a safety valve; instead, the Wall was breached for good.

In **Czechoslovakia** the police attacked a student march in Prague on 17 November 1989. A false rumour that a student had been killed spread; the universities were occupied and crowds filled the streets, while the police now stood by. Within a week the party leadership had resigned. Václav Havel and his Charter 77 friends formed **Civic Forum**, which within days became a shadow government. On 25 November half a million people gathered at Letná in Prague. The party's leading role was removed on 29 November; on 10 December a government with a non-Communist majority took office and Husák resigned. On 28 December the same Communist assembly that had once jailed Havel elected him President. Judt credits this "velvet revolution" to an opposition determined to avoid confrontation, a party whose bankruptcy was obvious, and Havel himself.

**Romania** was the exception. Ceauşescu had paid off the foreign debt by squeezing his people: energy was exported while Romanians used 40-watt bulbs. In December 1989 the Securitate tried to remove a Hungarian pastor, László Tőkés, in Timişoara; the vigil became a protest and troops fired on the crowd. On 21 December Ceauşescu was heckled into silence on a balcony in Bucharest; the next day he fled by helicopter. The army switched sides under a "National Salvation Front", and Ceauşescu and his wife were tried and shot on Christmas Day. The new president, Ion Iliescu, was a former Communist, and much of the old apparatus survived.

In **Bulgaria** the party removed its own leader. Todor Zhivkov, in power since 1954, had persecuted the Turkish minority; about 300,000 Turks left in the summer of 1989. On 10 November, the day after the Wall opened, reformers ousted him. This mattered because the fall of each regime made the next one seem possible, which meant that within two months every Soviet satellite in Europe had lost its Communist monopoly.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Mass protest brought down the hard-line regimes in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In both cases the regimes did not use full force, which Moscow's stance made unlikely.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The opening of the Wall was an accident of a regime trying to stabilise itself.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The exodus through Hungary had already made the border impossible to hold.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Romania and Bulgaria show that in some states Communists replaced their leaders rather than lost power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Romania's revolution began with a genuine popular revolt in Timişoara.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the fall of the Berlin Wall between 1989 and 1990.
Compare and contrast the ways in which Communist rule ended in Poland and Romania in 1989.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Berlin Wall fell because the East German regime, under pressure from emigration and protest, tried to stabilise itself and lost control.
useItInAnEssay.prove: After 22,000 people left through Hungary in three days and 300,000 marched in Leipzig, Schabowski announced on 9 November that travel was allowed at once.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a measure meant as a safety valve became an open border, since 50,000 people crossed within hours and the regime could not reverse it.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the regime was already doomed by the exodus, so the announcement only decided the timing.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The Wall therefore fell by accident, but the collapse it revealed was no accident.

chunks.title: Why so fast, and what followed, 1989–1993
chunks.body:
Why did Communism collapse so quickly? Judt warns against "retrospective determinism": few predicted the timing or manner of the end. Contagion explains part of it, since each fall weakened the next regime's claim to be inevitable. But all revolutions spread; the novelty of 1989 was **speed**. As late as October 1989, reformers in Hungary and East Germany thought they could manage their own perestroika. **Television** changed everything: people saw their own revolutions on the evening news, which destroyed the party's monopoly of information and the fear of being alone. And the revolutions were **peaceful**, Romania apart. The regimes' confidence in force was evaporating, the crowds rejected violence, and for most officials it seemed "better to swim with the current than be washed away".

What did people want instead? Judt's answer is "Europe". The European Community stood for rights, free movement and normal life. "The opposite of Communism was not 'capitalism' but 'Europe'." Civic Forum's programme ended with the words "Return to Europe".

The consequences unfolded quickly. **Germany** was unified. Chancellor Helmut Kohl proposed a five-year programme on 28 November 1989 but soon changed course: the flow west, at one point 2,000 people a day, could be stopped only by bringing West Germany east. In March 1990 the Alliance for Germany won 48 per cent in East German elections on a unification ticket; the Deutschmark arrived on 1 July; and on **3 October 1990** the GDR ceased to exist. Gorbachev, with 360,000 Soviet troops still in East Germany, had no good options. He settled for about $8 billion and $2 billion more in credits, while Kohl accepted Germany's eastern borders as permanent.

The bloc dissolved. By December 1989 the Warsaw Pact states were preparing publicly to renounce their 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia. New governments faced the painful transition to market economies, which the Poland section examines. Old national questions returned: Czechoslovakia itself divided peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on **1 January 1993**, the "velvet divorce", while Yugoslavia's break-up turned to war.

This mattered because Soviet control ended without a Soviet war, which meant that the peoples of central Europe could choose their own governments for the first time since 1945. Judt's judgement on the bloc's history is stark: once Moscow withdrew its guarantee, regimes that had lasted forty years were shown to have been "even weaker than anyone supposed".

argumentsThatWork.claim: Speed, television and the absence of violence distinguished 1989 from earlier revolutions.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Romania shows that violence was still possible where the regime chose it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: 'Europe' gave the revolutions a positive aim, not just an enemy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Nationalists cared more about Poland or Hungary than about Europe.

argumentsThatWork.claim: German unification and the end of the bloc depended on Gorbachev's acceptance.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Kohl and Washington drove unification; Gorbachev mainly set its price.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the consequences of the collapse of Soviet control for central and eastern Europe between 1989 and 1993.
To what extent was Gorbachev responsible for the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe in 1989?

useItInAnEssay.claim: German unification was the most important consequence of 1989, and it depended on Soviet acceptance.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In March 1990 the Alliance for Germany won 48 per cent on a unification ticket, and on 3 October 1990 the GDR ceased to exist, while 360,000 Soviet troops were still stationed there.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Moscow could in principle have blocked unification, so Gorbachev's decision to accept it, for about $8 billion, was decisive.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Judt shows that Gorbachev had no good options, since blocking unity would have destroyed his credibility, and Kohl and Washington drove the process.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Unification was therefore a Western initiative that succeeded because the Soviet Union had already given up control.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was Gorbachev responsible for the collapse of Soviet control in eastern Europe in 1989?
essayQuestions.scope: Eastern Europe; the collapse of Soviet control

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far Gorbachev, compared with debt, opposition and the regimes' weakness, caused the collapse

modelPlan.thesis: Gorbachev was largely responsible, because his renunciation of force removed the regimes' final guarantee; but debt, the survival of opposition and the regimes' loss of nerve explain why they fell once the guarantee was gone.

arguments.claim: Gorbachev removed the Soviet guarantee (named factor first).
Debt and economic failure left the regimes unable to buy calm.
Opposition survived and organised: Solidarity, Civic Forum.
Regimes lost confidence; television and speed did the rest.

modelPlan.counter: The regimes were already collapsing from within: Hungary's Communists dismantled their own system.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without Gorbachev, would the regimes have fallen in 1989? Unlikely, since force had saved them in 1953, 1956, 1968 and 1981.

segments.text: Gorbachev was largely responsible for the collapse of Soviet control in 1989, because he removed the regimes' final guarantee.
In December 1988 he told the UN that 'freedom of choice' had no exceptions, and in 1989 he told Jaruzelski that Solidarity's election victory must stand.
This meant that, unlike in 1956, 1968 or 1981, the regimes could not call on Soviet force when their people turned against them.
However, debt near $40 billion and years of organised opposition had already forced the Polish regime to negotiate before the election.
Gorbachev was therefore the decisive cause of the timing, while economic failure and opposition explain why the regimes had nothing left once Moscow let go.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The collapse of Communism in eastern Europe in 1989 was caused by economic failure.” Discuss.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far economic failure, rather than Moscow's withdrawal or opposition, caused the collapse

modelPlan.thesis: Economic failure was a necessary long-term condition, forcing the Polish regime to negotiate and stripping all the regimes of credibility; but it does not explain the timing, which came from Moscow's withdrawal of its guarantee.

arguments.claim: For: Poland's debt and price rises forced negotiation (named factor first).
For: Romania's austerity drove its people to revolt.
Against: Gorbachev's withdrawal of force decided the timing.
Against: speed, television and contagion.

modelPlan.counter: The economies had been failing for years without collapse, and Romania paid its debts but fell anyway.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did economic failure decide when Communism fell? No: it had existed for a decade, so it explains weakness, not timing.

segments.text: Economic failure made the collapse of Communism possible but did not decide when it came.
Poland's debt was approaching $40 billion, price rises of 25 and 60 per cent in 1987–88 provoked strikes, and in August 1988 the regime asked Wałęsa for help.
This meant that the Polish regime could no longer govern alone, so it opened the Round Table that ended its monopoly.
However, Romania had paid off its debt and still fell, and the regimes had survived economic crises before because Moscow stood behind them.
Economic failure was therefore a necessary cause, but Moscow's withdrawal was the sufficient one.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the fall of the Berlin Wall between 1989 and 1990.

decodeKey.scope: The fall of the Berlin Wall
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The Wall fell mainly because emigration through Hungary and mass protest made the border untenable, once Moscow refused to back Honecker; its decisive consequence was German unification in 1990.

arguments.claim: Cause: the exodus through Hungary.
Cause: Leipzig demonstrations and Gorbachev's refusal to save Honecker.
Consequence: the SED lost its leading role.
Consequence: German unification on 3 October 1990.

modelPlan.counter: The Wall was opened by accident, so its fall depended on a panicked announcement as much as on deeper causes.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence mattered most? Unification, because it ended the GDR and redrew Europe.

segments.text: The Berlin Wall fell because emigration and protest had already made the border impossible to hold.
After Hungary opened its border, some 22,000 East Germans crossed within 72 hours, and Leipzig's demonstrations grew to 300,000.
This meant the regime faced a choice between force and concession, and with Gorbachev warning that 'life punishes those who delay', it chose concession.
However, the actual opening on 9 November was an accident of Schabowski's announcement, which the rulers saw as stabilisation.
The Wall's fall was therefore accidental in form but inevitable in substance, and it led directly to unification in October 1990.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the ways in which Communist rule ended in Poland and Romania in 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: Both regimes fell in 1989 once Moscow withdrew its support, but Poland's ended by negotiation with a strong opposition, while Romania's ended in violence and a coup that left much of the old apparatus in place.

arguments.claim: Similarity: economic crisis and Moscow's withdrawal.
Similarity: popular anger at the regime.
Difference: negotiation and elections in Poland.
Difference: violence, execution and a former Communist president in Romania.

modelPlan.counter: In both countries members of the old regime kept influence: Jaruzelski became head of state in Poland, Iliescu president in Romania.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most for the future? The existence of an organised opposition, which made Poland's transition real and Romania's 'suspiciously smooth'.

segments.text: Communist rule ended in both Poland and Romania in 1989, but by opposite routes.
In Poland Round Table talks led to elections in which Solidarity won 99 of 100 Senate seats, whereas in Romania troops fired on crowds and Ceauşescu was executed on Christmas Day.
This meant that Poland had an organised opposition ready to govern, while in Romania power passed to the former Communist Iliescu and much of the old apparatus.
However, in both cases figures from the old regime kept influence, since Jaruzelski became Poland's head of state.
The decisive difference was therefore the strength of organised opposition, which shaped how far each country actually changed.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the role of popular protest in the end of Communist rule in Czechoslovakia and East Germany in 1989.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: How far protest, compared with Moscow's stance and the regimes' weakness, ended Communist rule

modelPlan.thesis: Popular protest was the immediate force that ended Communist rule in both countries, but it succeeded because the regimes would not or could not use force once Moscow had refused to support them.

arguments.claim: East Germany: Leipzig and Berlin demonstrations (named factor first).
Czechoslovakia: students and crowds at Letná.
The regimes' loss of nerve and Moscow's refusal to help.
Emigration and leadership: Hungary's border and Havel.

modelPlan.counter: In East Germany emigration did as much as protest to break the regime.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would the regimes have fallen without the crowds? Not in 1989, so protest was decisive for timing.

segments.text: Popular protest was the immediate cause of the end of Communist rule in East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
Leipzig's demonstrations grew to 300,000 and half a million gathered in Berlin on 4 November, while in Prague half a million gathered at Letná on 25 November.
This meant the regimes faced crowds too large to disperse without massacre, so they removed leaders and then surrendered their monopoly.
However, the crowds succeeded because Moscow would not back force, and in East Germany emigration through Hungary had already broken the regime.
Protest was therefore decisive, but only in a situation where force was no longer available.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the consequences of the collapse of Soviet control for central and eastern Europe between 1989 and 1993.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: The most important consequence was that the region's states could choose their own governments and alliances; German unification was the largest single change, and the return of national questions the most dangerous.

arguments.claim: German unification.
The end of the bloc and its renunciation of 1968.
Contested transitions: Romania's surviving apparatus.
National questions: Czechoslovakia's peaceful division.

modelPlan.counter: Many old elites survived the change, so the consequences were less revolutionary than they looked.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence changed Europe most? German unification, which ended the post-war division.

segments.text: The most important consequence of the collapse was that Germany was reunited and the post-war division of Europe ended.
On 3 October 1990 the GDR ceased to exist, after Gorbachev accepted unification for about $8 billion and Kohl recognised Germany's eastern borders.
This meant the central question of post-war Europe was settled peacefully, so the other states of the region could look to 'Europe' rather than Moscow.
However, in Romania much of the old apparatus survived under Iliescu, which shows the transition was uneven.
Unification was therefore the decisive consequence, while uneven transitions and national questions shaped the 1990s.
